title: Sis Ganj and Rakab Ganj
hook: where Guru Tegh Bahadur was killed and where his body was cremated

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bangla Sahib, where the child Guru went out to the sick, and the pool beside it. Your line was the child's gurdwara.

Car horns. A man pushing a cart stacked with sacks. A wedding-card shop, a sweet shop, a rickshaw wedged sideways in the lane. Old Delhi's great market street, Chandni Chowk, is loud from morning to night. And right in the middle of it, between the stalls, a gurdwara with a white front and a gold dome, its singing drifting out into the traffic. Across the city stands a second gurdwara tied to the same day. Two buildings, one death. Today, why it takes two.
screen: `CAR HORNS, CARTS, A SWEET SHOP.` → `A GURDWARA AMONG THE STALLS.` → `TWO BUILDINGS, ONE DEATH.`

segments.voice: First, Sis Ganj. Sis is the Punjabi word for head. Year one told the story: Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, would not give up his faith, nor let others be forced from theirs, and he was beheaded in the open square of Chandni Chowk. Gurdwara Sis Ganj stands at that spot, right in the market, and tradition says it keeps the trunk of the tree under which he was killed. Second, Rakab Ganj. This path has met both carriers: Bhai Jaita, who took the head north to Anandpur, and Lakhi Shah Vanjara, who took the body home and set his own house alight. Tradition says Gurdwara Rakab Ganj stands where that house burned. Third, why two. Danger split the Guru's body two ways, and the panth would not lose either. It marked the place of the death and the place of the fire, and kept walking to both: one in the loud middle of a market, open to anyone between errands, the other marking a fire lit in secret by a man with a cart. Fourth, a line from the Guru's own saloks near the end of the Granth, in paraphrase: whatever has come into being will pass away, today or tomorrow; so sing the praises of the Lord, and let the other tangles go. He wrote about the body passing. Then his own body passed, and two ordinary men made sure it was honored. Two addresses for one gift.
screen: `SIS GANJ: WHERE HE GAVE HIS HEAD.` · `RAKAB GANJ: WHERE THE HOUSE BURNED.` · `TWO PLACES, NEITHER LOST.` · `WHATEVER COMES INTO BEING PASSES.` · then, large: `TWO ADDRESSES FOR ONE GIFT.`

segments.voice: Hear the horns, the carts, the shopkeepers calling, and let the noise be there. Then walk, in your mind, through the open doors of Sis Ganj and let the noise fall behind you, standing quietly where the market once watched a man refuse to be moved. Step back out into the street carrying a little of that quiet, and if you pray, rest on Waheguru.
Sis Ganj and Rakab Ganj. Two gurdwaras in Delhi: one where Guru Tegh Bahadur was beheaded, one where his body was secretly cremated. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: where he gave his head. He stood firm for other people's freedom as well as his own. Go gently.

howItsDone: Sikhs visiting Delhi go to Gurdwara Sis Ganj in Chandni Chowk and Gurdwara Rakab Ganj, and both are crowded on the day Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom is remembered.

notes: Days 79, 80, 155, 871 and 976 told the martyrdom, the carrying of the head, the marking of the sites and the Rakab Ganj wall. Today's angle: one death, two places, and who did the carrying.
'This path met both carriers on earlier days' refers to days 1319 (Lakhi Shah) and 1321 (Bhai Jaita); checked by the editor.
'Tradition says it keeps the trunk of the tree under which he was killed': please confirm Sis Ganj preserves the tree trunk.

Ang 1429, salok 52 ('jo upjio so binas hai parou aaj kai kaal; naanak har gun gaae le chhaad sagal janjaal') paraphrased; please confirm salok number and Ang. Salok 16 (frighten no one, fear no one) was avoided because it is used often on this path.
'Sis is the Punjabi word for head' is a word meaning, not an etymology; the meaning of 'Rakab' is deliberately not given.
Original ਸੀਸ ਗੰਜ: please confirm spelling.
